title: Room 402
setting: A couple arrives at 9pm and the hotel is overbooked by one.

lines.t: Good evening. We have a reservation for two nights, the name is Ivanov.
Let me check... I'm very sorry. We're overbooked and there's no room tonight.
We booked six weeks ago.
You did, and this is our mistake, not a problem with your booking.
So what happens now?
I've held a room at our partner hotel, four minutes away, and we pay the taxi.
And tomorrow?
Room 402 here, sea view, at the rate you originally booked.
That's better than I expected, honestly.
I'd rather tell you straight than hide behind the word 'system'.

title: Overbooked by three
setting: Three more guests than rooms, and someone has to be told.

lines.t: We're overbooked by three rooms tonight.
How did that happen?
Two walk-ins at six, and the coach party arrived complete. Usually one reservation turns into a no-show.
Who has checked in already?
Everyone except the three late arrivals.
Then those three are the ones we phone. Not the family, and not the man who's here every month.
The couple with the booking reference ending 40. They arrive at ten.
Put them in the Rila, upgrade them to a suite there, and make the transfer complimentary.
That costs us ninety leva.
A guest turned away badly costs us four years. Have the concierge arrange the taxi personally.
And tomorrow?
We're fully booked again, so a room has to be free by noon. Whoever agrees to check out early gets a coffee and a thank you.

title: Room 214
setting: One room got missed on a full day.

lines.t: Room 214 says the amenities weren't replaced.
Housekeeping did that floor at eleven.
Then somebody skipped one room, which happens on a full day.
Shall I send someone up?
Now, with the missing items and an apology at the door.
She also asked about room service after ten.
The kitchen closes at ten thirty. Tell her honestly and offer the bar menu until midnight.
And the turndown service?
Top floor only, and only while guests are out. Never knock at nine at night on somebody's holiday.
Understood. I'll take the towels up myself.

title: November at the same price
setting: The hotel is full in August and empty in November.

lines.t: Our occupancy rate in November was 38%.
And in August?
Ninety-four. Peak season pays for the rest of the year.
So the off season is the problem.
The problem is charging off season prices without changing what's in the offer.
What would you change?
Half board included instead of a discount. Full board for anyone staying five nights.
That's a package deal, and it costs us less than dropping the rate.
And the restaurant is empty in November anyway.
All-inclusive as well?
No. That brings people who never leave the hotel, and the town needs them too.
Then push the loyalty programme at the same time, and keep two of the seasonal staff through the winter.

title: A nut allergy on a full Saturday
setting: A waiter takes an order on the busiest night of the year.

lines.t: Before we order, I should say I have a serious nut allergy.
Thank you for telling me. I'll write it in red and repeat it to the kitchen.
Even a small amount is a problem.
Understood. Are you happy for me to check each dish with the chef?
Please do.
The starters are fine. I'd avoid the dessert with the crumb topping.
Is there an alternative?
The sorbet, and I'll confirm the whole ticket with the pastry section.
You've done this before.
Every allergy gets read back twice. It takes eight seconds and it matters.

title: Table nine
setting: Eighty-four covers booked and one table with a serious allergy.

lines.t: How many covers tonight?
Eighty-four booked. Peak times are seven to nine, as always.
Then front of house needs four people at seven, not three.
Table nine has dietary requirements.
Which ones?
One serious nut allergy.
Then you tell the kitchen yourself, out loud, and you watch that plate leave back of house.
I've taken the order and written it down.
Write it and say it. Paper doesn't hear you.
They'll want to split the bill. Six people from three companies.
Then ask before dessert rather than after, and check the service charge is explained on the menu.
And last orders?
Ten thirty, said politely at ten fifteen, so nobody feels pushed out of the door.

title: The room above the kitchen
setting: Three bad nights that nobody heard about until checkout.

lines.t: A guest complaint from 305. Noise from the kitchen extractor, three nights running.
Three nights, and she's telling us now?
She says she didn't want to be difficult.
Those are the ones we lose without ever knowing why.
What do I offer?
Move her tonight, apologise for the inconvenience once, and compensate her for the three nights.
A voucher, or a refund?
Ask her. A refund if she's leaving, a voucher if she's coming back.
And the man in 210 who's complained about everything since Monday?
High maintenance, and still a guest. Solve what's solvable and stop apologising for the weather.
He left a jacket in the restaurant, by the way.
Lost property, logged and labelled. Then go the extra mile for a guest who's easy to please, because those are the ones who come back.

title: The seven o'clock transfer
setting: A guest checks tomorrow's plan at the concierge desk.

lines.t: Can you look at our itinerary for tomorrow?
Of course. The transfer to the airport is at seven.
That's very early.
Your flight is at ten, there's a layover in Vienna, and the desk closes at nine.
And today?
The guided tour leaves at ten from the front steps. Two hours, four landmarks, and the guide's English is excellent.
My husband would rather go sightseeing on his own.
Then here's a map with the same four places and their opening times.
Can we print our boarding passes here?
At the desk, any time before six tomorrow.
We'll be exhausted. It's a five-hour difference.
Jet lag is easier if you stay up until ten tonight. Everybody tells you to sleep early, and it makes the second day worse.
